newsitem.title: GERMANY: Issing not fully satisfied with EMU pact -report.
newsitem.headline: Issing not fully satisfied with EMU pact -report.

text.p: Bundesbank chief economist Otmar Issing said he was not satisfied with the lack of "automaticity" in the stability pact for monetary union agreed by European leaders last Friday, the Financial Times reported on Tuesday.

Issing told the British newspaper: "Unrestrained automaticity would not have been possible but one cannot be satisfied with a decision mechanism in which potential sinners pass judgement on actual sinners."
Germany had originally sought fully automatic sanctions for countries failing to keep their budgets under control during currency union, but agreed on a compromise.
Issing also told the newspaper that he feared the future European central bank could be overburdened in carrying out its task of maintaining price stability.
"The danger that too much pressure would be put on the monetary policy of the European central bank has not been eliminated," he said.

Issing said the stability pact, hailed by Chancellor Helmut Kohl as a triumph for its initiator, German Finance Minister Theo Waigel, needed further refinement in order to minimise political interference in monitoring fiscal stability under the common currency, which is scheduled for launch in Januray 1999.
"The hard task ahead will be to implement the pact in such a way that it wil be difficult to make purely political decisions .... The debate is not over yet," he said.
However Issing said the important message of the pact was to achieve a balanced budget throughout the European monetary region in the medium term.
"If you take that seriously, this is a huge step forward," Issing told the newspaper.
